title: Astro Introduces Sätteri: A Rust-powered Markdown And Mdx Processor With Up To 60% Faster Builds
author: Daniel Curtis
gist: Astro made Sätteri, a Rust-based Markdown/MDX processor built by contributor Erika, the default engine in Astro 7.0, replacing the unified/remark/rehype JavaScript pipeline and delivering 15-61% faster builds, part of a broader industry trend of native-language rewrites of JS toolchain internals for speed.

themes.theme: Native-language rewrite drives concrete build speedups

insights.claim: Sätteri, a Rust-based Markdown/MDX processor built on pulldown-cmark for CommonMark parsing and Oxc for MDX expression parsing, became the default processor in Astro 7.0 and contributes up to 60% faster builds according to the Astro team.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Another data point in the broader JS-tooling trend of rewriting hot-path internals in Rust/Zig for order-of-magnitude speedups (alongside Vite, Turbopack, Biome, etc.) — signals continued migration of JS ecosystem performance-critical code away from JavaScript itself.
insights.quote: Sätteri, a new high-performance Markdown and MDX processor for the JavaScript ecosystem, has been introduced by the Astro team and now sits at the heart of the recently released Astro 7.0... Sätteri lives outside the Astro organisation but has become a core dependency of the framework, where the team says it contributes up to 60% faster builds.

insights.claim: Switching the Astro and Cloudflare documentation sites to Sätteri shaved over a minute off each build, and overall Astro 7 builds improved by 15 to 61%, with much of the gain coming from moving parsing out of JavaScript and replacing the unified pipeline of remark, rehype, and a long tail of dependencies that previously ran plugin after plugin over the full syntax tree.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Concrete, named production case studies (Astro docs, Cloudflare docs) validating the speedup claim, useful evidence for other doc-heavy static-site operators evaluating a migration to Astro 7 / Sätteri for build-cost reduction.
insights.quote: switching the Astro and Cloudflare documentation sites to Sätteri shaved over a minute off each build, and overall Astro 7 builds improved by 15 to 61%

insights.claim: Sätteri natively implements features that previously required separate plugins in the unified ecosystem, including GitHub Flavored Markdown, smart punctuation, container directives, math, frontmatter, superscript, subscript, and wikilinks, reducing dependency count by roughly 100 packages according to its author.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Consolidating previously plugin-fragmented features into one native processor reduces supply-chain surface area (fewer npm dependencies) — a secondary security/maintenance benefit beyond raw speed that's relevant to software supply-chain risk discussions.
insights.quote: a pipeline that's faster (and about 100 deps leaner) felt like a better default

insights.claim: Sätteri ships platform-specific native binaries with a WASM fallback, the same distribution approach Astro uses for its new Rust compiler, and can be tried live in-browser via WebAssembly.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Native-binary-plus-WASM-fallback is becoming the standard distribution pattern for Rust-based JS tooling, a packaging template other framework authors doing similar native rewrites are likely to replicate.
insights.quote: It ships platform-specific native binaries with a WASM fallback, the same approach Astro uses for its new Rust compiler, and it can be tried live in the browser via WebAssembly.

themes.theme: Ecosystem fragmentation risk and community pushback

insights.claim: A Hacker News commenter criticized the move away from the widely-supported unified/rehype ecosystem toward Astro's own rehype-incompatible tooling purely for build-speed gains, expressing skepticism that the compatibility shim added to keep using rehype will last.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Highlights a recurring tension in JS tooling: performance-driven native rewrites risk ecosystem fragmentation and plugin-compatibility debt, a factor for teams with heavy existing remark/rehype plugin investments to weigh before adopting Astro 7's new default.
insights.quote: Switch from widely supported unified/rehype to own rehype-incompatible markdown tooling just for build time speed improvement is quite upsetting. Good that they added a tool to keep using rehype, but I'm unsure that it will last

insights.claim: Sätteri author Erika stated the team does not intend to remove support for the unified ecosystem and deliberately made the Markdown processing pipeline pluggable so both approaches can coexist, noting the vast majority of users don't use unified plugins, making the faster, leaner pipeline a better default.
insights.speaker: Erika (quoted by Daniel Curtis)
insights.so_what: A vendor commitment to backward compatibility (via @astrojs/markdown-remark) reduces migration risk for the minority of users on custom remark/rehype plugins, an important reassurance for enterprise adopters evaluating the Astro 7 upgrade.
insights.quote: We don't intend on removing support for the unified ecosystem, we on purpose made the Markdown processing pipeline pluggable so that it was possible for both to exists! The vast majority of our users don't use any sort of unified plugins

insights.claim: Projects without existing remark/rehype plugins need no changes to adopt Sätteri under Astro 7, while projects depending on plugins can port them to Sätteri's MDAST/HAST plugin format or opt out entirely by installing the @astrojs/markdown-remark package; upgrades are handled via npx @astrojs/upgrade.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Concrete, low-friction migration path (opt-out package plus an automated upgrade CLI) lowers the practical barrier to Astro 7 adoption even for teams with existing plugin dependencies.
insights.quote: The Astro v7 upgrade guide advises that projects without plugins need no changes, while those depending on plugins can port them to Sätteri MDAST or HAST plugins or stay on unified by installing @astrojs/markdown-remark. Upgrades are handled with npx @astrojs/upgrade.

themes.theme: Competitive landscape in native Markdown processing

insights.claim: Sätteri is not alone in chasing native Markdown speed: Bun.markdown, written in Zig, has reported comparable performance gains but lacks a plugin system, leaving Sätteri's reuse of the unified AST format as its distinguishing feature.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Identifies a competitive field forming around native (Rust/Zig) Markdown processors for JS toolchains; Sätteri's AST compatibility with the existing unified ecosystem is a specific differentiation angle versus Bun's plugin-less approach, relevant to which library becomes the ecosystem standard.
insights.quote: Sätteri is not alone in chasing native Markdown speed. Bun.markdown, written in Zig, has reported comparable gains but lacks a plugin system, leaving Sätteri's reuse of the unified AST format as a distinguishing feature.

insights.claim: Per benchmarks the author (Erika) linked, marked is very lightweight but slower than both Sätteri and markdown-it (and its forks); Sätteri reuses the same AST format as the unified ecosystem, which may make it more extensibility-friendly than marked.
insights.speaker: Erika (quoted by Daniel Curtis)
insights.so_what: Gives a relative performance/extensibility ranking among JS Markdown libraries (marked vs markdown-it vs Sätteri) useful for engineering teams choosing a Markdown processor independent of the Astro-specific context.
insights.quote: The TL;DR is that marked is very light, but a bit on the slower side compared to Sätteri and markdown-it (and its forks).
insights.locator: quoted reply from Erika on marked comparison
